name: Scleral whitening / conjunctivectomy

lead: Scleral whitening, also called cosmetic eye whitening or conjunctivectomy, is an elective operation to make the white of the eye look whiter by removing or treating the surface tissue that carries blood vessels. One branded version is called I-BRITE. The visible change is the goal of the procedure itself once healed.

As described in case literature, it involves dissecting the conjunctiva and Tenon's capsule, applying cautery and using mitomycin C, an agent that limits tissue regrowth, to keep vessels and redness from returning. The published material consists mainly of case reports; no controlled trials of the cosmetic procedure were found.

paras: It is a surgical procedure done by an eye surgeon in a clinic or operating setting, followed by a healing period before the final look shows.

A case report describes severe pain, scleral inflammation and necrosis in both eyes nine years after the procedure, treated with immunosuppressive therapy. Another describes recurrent conjunctival redness five years afterward, and one patient used painted contact lenses to mask returning redness.

angle.text: This elective surgery, sold under names like I-BRITE, removes or cauterises conjunctival tissue so fewer vessels show and the whites of the eyes look whiter after healing. Published reports are mostly case reports of late complications.

lead: Scleral whitening, also called cosmetic eye whitening or cosmetic conjunctivectomy, is an elective eye procedure meant to make the white of the eye look whiter and clearer by removing the conjunctival tissue and its visible blood vessels. People seek it when chronic redness or prominent vessels make the eyes look tired or irritated, because the whites of the eyes strongly influence how bright and healthy the face looks. One commercially named version is I-BRITE [1][2].

Published descriptions say the surgery was introduced in 2008 and then popularized in South Korea, and that it involves removing conjunctiva (with Tenon's capsule), then applying mitomycin C 0.02%, an antiproliferative drug, so that the area heals as bleached-looking, vessel-free sclera [3][4]. A 2013 cohort review covered 1713 subjects treated by one surgeon with postoperative mitomycin C, with or without bevacizumab injection [5].
The published literature is mainly case reports and case series on complications, including scleral thinning, necrotizing scleritis, dry eye and recurrence of redness [1][3][4][6].

paras: Case reports describe the procedure as dissection of the conjunctiva and Tenon's capsule, cautery and application of mitomycin C, performed for cosmetic reasons in people who dislike visible redness or blood vessels on the white of the eye [1]. The term conjunctivectomy refers to surgical removal of conjunctival tissue. Patients were treated for chronic conjunctival hyperemia, the persistent redness of the white of the eye [3].

A 2017 review states that cosmetic eye whitening was introduced in 2008 and subsequently popularized in South Korea [3]. A 2013 study reviewed records of 1713 consecutive subjects who received cosmetic wide conjunctivectomy plus topical mitomycin C from November 2007 to May 2010 [5].

The 2017 review lists chronic conjunctival epithelial defects, scleral thinning, avascular zones in the sclera, dry eye and diplopia needing strabismus surgery among reported complications, and says the evidence on efficacy and safety is limited [3].

A 2015 report described a 33-year-old man who developed bilateral scleral thinning and calcific deposits four years after I-BRITE [4]. A 2018 case series from South Korea identified 4 patients with necrotizing scleritis among 231 who had received cosmetic eye whitening, at an average of 51 months after surgery, all needing systemic anti-inflammatory treatment [6].

A 2023 case report described a 36-year-old woman who developed severe pain, scleral inflammation and necrosis in both eyes nine years after an I-BRITE procedure; she improved with immunosuppressive therapy [1]. A 2020 case report described a 37-year-old man with recurrent redness five years after the procedure, who was fitted with white-painted scleral contact lenses to mask regrown vessels with a reported good cosmetic result [2].
No controlled trials found. Human evidence consists of a 2013 cohort review of 1713 subjects [5], a 2018 retrospective case series [6], a 2017 review [3] and individual case reports [1][2][4].
